title: Factoring Trigonometric Equations
subject: mathematics

theory.introduction: Many trigonometric equations can be solved by treating trigonometric expressions such as sin(x), cos(x), or tan(x) like algebraic variables. The key idea is to rearrange the equation so that it can be factored, apply the Zero Product Property, solve every resulting trigonometric equation, and then combine all valid solutions. Factoring is especially useful for equations containing products, common factors, or quadratic expressions in a trigonometric function.

content.text: If a product equals zero, at least one factor must equal zero. This allows a complicated trigonometric equation to be separated into simpler equations.
Move all terms to one side, factor the expression, solve each factor, and combine all valid solutions.

formulas.name: Zero Product Property
formulas.explanation: The main rule used after factoring a trigonometric equation. Every factor must be set equal to zero.

formulas.name: Zero Product Property for Three Factors
formulas.expression: ABC = 0  ⇒  A = 0 or B = 0 or C = 0
formulas.explanation: The same principle applies when an equation has three or more factors.

formulas.name: Common-Factor Pattern
formulas.explanation: Factor out the common expression before solving. The common factor may be sin(x), cos(x), tan(x), or another trigonometric expression.

formulas.name: Difference of Squares
formulas.explanation: Useful when a trigonometric equation contains the difference between two squares.

formulas.name: Perfect Square Trinomials
formulas.expression: A² + 2AB + B² = (A + B)²;  A² − 2AB + B² = (A − B)²
formulas.explanation: Useful when a trigonometric expression forms a perfect-square trinomial.

formulas.name: Quadratic Factoring Pattern
formulas.expression: u² + bu + c = (u + p)(u + q), where p + q = b and pq = c
formulas.explanation: A trigonometric expression such as cos²(x) + bcos(x) + c can be treated algebraically by temporarily viewing cos(x) as the variable u.

formulas.name: Quadratic Zero Form
formulas.explanation: Rewrite a trigonometric equation into zero form before attempting to factor.

formulas.name: Sine Equals Zero
formulas.explanation: Useful when sin(x) appears as a factor.

formulas.name: Cosine Equals Zero
formulas.expression: cos(x) = 0  ⇒  x = π/2 + nπ,  n ∈ ℤ
formulas.explanation: Useful when cos(x) appears as a factor.

formulas.name: Tangent Equals Zero
formulas.explanation: Useful when tan(x) appears as a factor.

formulas.name: Sine Equals One-Half
formulas.explanation: A common result when factoring equations involving sin(x).

formulas.name: Sine Equals Negative One-Half
formulas.explanation: Useful when a factored equation produces sin(x) = −1/2.

formulas.name: Cosine Equals One-Half
formulas.explanation: A common result when factoring equations involving cos(x).

formulas.name: Cosine Equals Negative One-Half
formulas.explanation: Useful when a factored equation produces cos(x) = −1/2.

formulas.name: Range of Sine
formulas.explanation: Any factor that produces sin(x) outside this range has no real solution.

formulas.name: Range of Cosine
formulas.explanation: Any factor that produces cos(x) outside this range has no real solution.

formulas.name: Range of Tangent
formulas.explanation: Tangent can take every real value, although it is undefined where cos(x) = 0.

formulas.name: Period of Sine
formulas.explanation: Sine repeats every 2π radians, which is why general solutions commonly contain 2nπ.

formulas.name: Period of Cosine
formulas.explanation: Cosine repeats every 2π radians.

formulas.name: Period of Tangent
formulas.explanation: Tangent repeats every π radians, so general tangent solutions commonly contain nπ.

formulas.name: Division by a Possible-Zero Factor
formulas.expression: If A(x)B(x) = 0, do not divide by A(x) without separately considering A(x) = 0.
formulas.explanation: Dividing by an expression that may equal zero can remove valid solutions.

formulas.name: Union of Factor Solutions
formulas.expression: Solutions of A(x)B(x)=0 = solutions of A(x)=0 ∪ solutions of B(x)=0
formulas.explanation: The final answer contains every valid solution from every factor.

examples.question: Solve 2sin²(x) − sin(x) = 0 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: Factor: sin(x)(2sin(x) − 1) = 0. Apply the Zero Product Property: sin(x) = 0 or 2sin(x) − 1 = 0. First, sin(x) = 0 gives x = 0, π in the interval. Second, 2sin(x) − 1 = 0 gives sin(x) = 1/2, so x = π/6, 5π/6. Therefore the solutions are x = 0, π/6, 5π/6, π.

examples.question: Solve 3cos²(x) − 3cos(x) = 0 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: Factor out 3cos(x): 3cos(x)(cos(x) − 1) = 0. Therefore cos(x) = 0 or cos(x) = 1. On 0 ≤ x < 2π, cos(x) = 0 gives x = π/2, 3π/2, while cos(x) = 1 gives x = 0. Final answer: x = 0, π/2, 3π/2.

examples.question: Solve 2sin²(x) + sin(x) = 0 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: Factor: sin(x)(2sin(x) + 1) = 0. Therefore sin(x) = 0 or sin(x) = −1/2. On 0 ≤ x < 2π, sin(x) = 0 gives x = 0, π. Sin(x) = −1/2 gives x = 7π/6, 11π/6. Final answer: x = 0, π, 7π/6, 11π/6.

examples.question: Solve cos²(x) − 3cos(x) + 2 = 0 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: Treat cos(x) like an algebraic variable. Factor: (cos(x) − 1)(cos(x) − 2) = 0. Therefore cos(x) = 1 or cos(x) = 2. Cos(x) = 2 has no real solution because −1 ≤ cos(x) ≤ 1. Cos(x) = 1 gives x = 0 in the interval. Final answer: x = 0.

examples.question: Solve sin²(x) − 1 = 0 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: Use the difference of squares: sin²(x) − 1 = (sin(x) − 1)(sin(x) + 1) = 0. Therefore sin(x) = 1 or sin(x) = −1. On 0 ≤ x < 2π, these give x = π/2 and x = 3π/2. Final answer: x = π/2, 3π/2.

examples.question: Solve (2sin(x) − 1)(cos(x) + 1) = 0 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: Set each factor equal to zero. 2sin(x) − 1 = 0 gives sin(x) = 1/2, so x = π/6, 5π/6. Cos(x) + 1 = 0 gives cos(x) = −1, so x = π. Combine all valid solutions: x = π/6, 5π/6, π.

examples.question: Solve (cos(x) − 2)(sin(x) + 1) = 0.
examples.solution: Set each factor equal to zero. cos(x) − 2 = 0 gives cos(x) = 2, which has no real solution because cosine lies between −1 and 1. sin(x) + 1 = 0 gives sin(x) = −1, so x = 3π/2 + 2nπ, n ∈ ℤ. Therefore the general solution is x = 3π/2 + 2nπ.

examples.question: Solve 2sin²(x) − sin(x) = 0 for all real x.
examples.solution: Factor: sin(x)(2sin(x) − 1) = 0. Thus sin(x) = 0 or sin(x) = 1/2. For sin(x) = 0, x = nπ. For sin(x) = 1/2, x = π/6 + 2nπ or x = 5π/6 + 2nπ, where n ∈ ℤ. These three families form the complete general solution.

examples.question: Solve sin(x)(2sin(x) − 1) = 0 and explain why dividing by sin(x) is dangerous.
examples.solution: Factoring already gives sin(x) = 0 or 2sin(x) − 1 = 0. Therefore both sin(x) = 0 and sin(x) = 1/2 must be solved. If we divide by sin(x), we get 2sin(x) − 1 = 0, but this assumes sin(x) ≠ 0 and removes all solutions where sin(x) = 0. The correct approach is to use the Zero Product Property.

examples.question: Solve 2sin²(x) = sin(x) for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: Move everything to one side: 2sin²(x) − sin(x) = 0. Factor: sin(x)(2sin(x) − 1) = 0. Thus sin(x) = 0 or sin(x) = 1/2. The solutions are x = 0, π, π/6, 5π/6. Ordered from smallest to largest: x = 0, π/6, 5π/6, π.

examples.question: Solve tan²(x) − tan(x) = 0 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: Factor: tan(x)(tan(x) − 1) = 0. Therefore tan(x) = 0 or tan(x) = 1. On 0 ≤ x < 2π, tan(x) = 0 gives x = 0, π. Tan(x) = 1 gives x = π/4, 5π/4. Final answer: x = 0, π/4, π, 5π/4.

examples.question: Solve sin(x)(sin(x) − 1)(sin(x) + 1) = 0 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: Set every factor equal to zero: sin(x) = 0, sin(x) = 1, or sin(x) = −1. On 0 ≤ x < 2π these give x = 0, π; x = π/2; and x = 3π/2. Final answer: x = 0, π/2, π, 3π/2.

examples.question: Factor and solve sin(x)cos(x) + 2sin(x) + 3cos(x) + 6 = 0.
examples.solution: Group terms: [sin(x)cos(x) + 2sin(x)] + [3cos(x) + 6] = 0. Factor each group: sin(x)[cos(x) + 2] + 3[cos(x) + 2] = 0. Factor again: [sin(x) + 3][cos(x) + 2] = 0. This would require sin(x) = −3 or cos(x) = −2. Neither is possible for real x because sine and cosine both lie between −1 and 1. Therefore there are no real solutions.

examples.question: Solve 4cos²(x) − 4 = 0 for 0 ≤ x < 2π.
examples.solution: Factor: 4(cos²(x) − 1) = 0. Use difference of squares: 4(cos(x) − 1)(cos(x) + 1) = 0. Therefore cos(x) = 1 or cos(x) = −1. On 0 ≤ x < 2π, x = 0 for cos(x) = 1 and x = π for cos(x) = −1. Final answer: x = 0, π.

key_ideas: Move all terms to one side before factoring whenever possible.
The Zero Product Property is the central rule after factoring.
Treat sin(x), cos(x), and tan(x) like algebraic variables when the equation has a suitable algebraic structure.
Factor out common trigonometric factors before using more complicated identities.
Use difference of squares when an expression has the form A² − B².
A factor can produce an impossible trigonometric value, such as sin(x) = 2 or cos(x) = −3; such a factor has no real solutions.
The final answer is the union of the solutions from every factor.
Do not divide by a trigonometric expression that might equal zero without separately checking that case.
When a restricted interval is given, keep only solutions inside that interval.
When no interval is given, use general solutions with n ∈ ℤ.
Always pay attention to the period of the trigonometric function being solved.
Check the original equation when transformations may have introduced domain issues or extraneous solutions.
Factoring connects algebraic equations with trigonometric equations and prepares the learner for quadratic trigonometric equations.
misconceptions: Dividing by sin(x) or cos(x) without checking whether that expression can equal zero.
Solving only the first factor and forgetting the remaining factors.
Thinking that A·B = 0 means A = 0 and B = 0 simultaneously.
Forgetting to move all terms to one side before applying the Zero Product Property.
Assuming every algebraic value obtained for sin(x) or cos(x) is possible.
Forgetting that sin(x) and cos(x) can only take values from −1 to 1.
Forgetting that tangent is undefined where cos(x) = 0.
Giving only one angle when a trigonometric equation has multiple solutions in the required interval.
Using the wrong period when writing general solutions.
Including an excluded endpoint such as 2π when the interval is 0 ≤ x < 2π.
Listing duplicate solutions when two different factors produce the same angle.
Assuming factoring automatically means there is a solution from every factor.
Stopping after factoring instead of solving each resulting trigonometric equation.
Using the factored equation for checking when an earlier algebraic operation may have changed the domain.
Confusing 'or' from the Zero Product Property with 'and'.
